transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Forecasters say Hurricane Isaias has now become a major Category 3 hurricane.
Top sustained winds are 120 miles per hour.
The storm is 170 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River.
The Secretary of Homeland Security is defending ICE agents who shot and wounded a migrant
man from the Dominican Republic yesterday in New York City.
Secretary Mark Wayne Mullen says the migrant should not be in the United States.
He blamed jurisdictions such as New York for allowing them to remain.
Through ICE and DHS, our men and women out there every day, we're enforcing our nation's
laws.
Not picking and choosing which laws to enforce, like the sanctuary politicians, we're enforcing
our nation's laws.
Why is that controversial?
When ICE agents fired into the man's car yesterday, Mullen says they did not know a five-year-old
child was also in the vehicle.
The child was not injured.
New York officials have protested over the incident.
It's not clear why the ICE agents opened fire.
ICE opened higher this morning as crude oil prices dip, NPR's Scott Horsley reports.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose about 150 points in early trading.
Oil prices backed off their recent highs after President Trump said he would not order widespread
military strikes on Iran until after the midterm elections next month.
The average price of gasoline in the U.S. inched up about a penny per gallon overnight,
while diesel prices dipped by a similar amount.
The World Trade Organization has raised its forecast for global trade this year, despite
the disruption caused by fighting in the Middle East.
The WTO says importers and exporters are adjusting to the conflict, while the artificial intelligence
boom continues to drive up demand.
And mortgage rates have climbed to their highest level in almost three years.
Freddie Mac says the average rate on a 30-year home loan is now 7.4 percent.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
Authorities in Russia say they've lifted public health restrictions following the death of
a 28-year-old lab worker at a plague research institute in Siberia.
And Perot's Charles Mains reports this has raised concerns about a potential outbreak
of plague.
Ever since the death of a female lab technician in Russia's Irkutsk region last week, Russian
health authorities have insisted she succumbed to an unknown form of pneumonia rather than
the plague.
Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobsov, all but declared that version final.
Kobsov said the deceased lab technician had been vaccinated and was immune to the deadly
pathogen she worked with.
He also said thousands of tests found no evidence of infection among other lab workers and that
life in Irkutsk would be going back to normal.
The de facto declaration of an end to the investigation comes despite calls by the World
Health Organization and the White House for more Russian transparency about the case.
NPR's Charles Mains.
This is NPR.
The winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize is former United Nations human rights chief
and international jurist Navi Pillay.
She led a UN inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
The Israeli Foreign Ministry condemned the choice today.
It said the Nobel Committee has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century.
In the U.S., Curtis Flowers has died.
The Mississippi man was at the center of a national debate on racial bias in jury selection.
He was tried multiple times for the same crime; eventually he had his death sentence tossed
out by the U.S. Supreme Court.
Gaylene James of Mississippi Public Broadcasting has more.
Curtis Flowers spent more than 22 years behind bars wrongly accused of murder.
Flowers, who was black, was charged in the 1996 killings of four people at a furniture
store in Winona, Mississippi.
Over the next two decades, prosecutors tried him six times.
Then, in 2019, the Supreme Court threw out his conviction, ruling that prosecutors improperly
excluded black jurors.
Flowers was 26 when he was arrested.
He was 50 when Mississippi dropped the charges against him in 2020.
He was 56 when he died at home on Wednesday.
No cause of death has been released.
In a statement, lawyers for Curtis Flowers write, "His name is etched into the U.S. Supreme
Court jurisprudence," about what it means to fight for a fair trial free from racial
bias and the selection of jurors.
For NPR News, I'm Gaylene James in Jackson, Mississippi.
It's NPR.
